planting.note: Direct-sow in fall to let winter provide natural stratification into sharply drained, low-fertility soil; deadhead spent spikes to extend bloom and limit self-seeding.

directions: A Pacific Northwest native with unusually variable flower color ranging from blue-purple to pink to yellow-cream, this penstemon naturalizes well in dry-to-moist meadows and serves as a host plant for Edith's checkerspot and Chalcedon checkerspot butterflies. It needs sharp drainage and low-fertility soil but tolerates both dry slopes and moist subalpine meadows. Deadhead spent spikes to extend bloom and prevent excessive self-seeding in smaller beds.

planting.note: Direct-sow with cold stratification into a deep gritty scree mix topped with pea gravel; protect from winter wet rather than cold, since this is a raised-bed or trough specialist.

directions: A true alpine cushion plant endemic to Colorado's highest peaks, this species carries extremely showy pale-blue to purple flowers on a mat barely a few inches tall, ideal for trough and scree rock gardens. Replicate alpine talus with a deep gritty scree mix of more than fifty percent mineral grit and a top-dress of pea gravel to keep the crown dry. It is far more cold-hardy than moisture-tolerant, so protect it from winter wet rather than cold, best achieved in raised beds or troughs where drainage can be guaranteed.

planting.note: Direct-sow with 6 weeks cold stratification onto a gravelly slope or berm; this species resents heavy or wet winter soils above almost anything else.

directions: One of the earliest-blooming penstemons, flowering as early as April, this species carries striking waxy blue-gray foliage that stays ornamental even out of bloom, topped with azure flowers on compact plants. Site on a gravelly slope or berm, since this species resents heavy or wet winter soils above almost anything else. The blue-gray foliage pairs well with other early bloomers in a rock garden; watch for powdery mildew in humid springs, which good airflow prevents.

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or sow stratified seed in spring into lean, sagebrush-steppe-style soil; avoid rich garden soil and summer irrigation, which encourage rot.

directions: A low, semi-evergreen shrub from Columbia Basin shrub-steppe, this species offers structure and winter interest rare among herbaceous penstemons, with lavender-pink flowers attracting bees and hummingbirds. Because it is woody-based and semi-evergreen, prune lightly in early spring to remove winter dieback rather than cutting hard to the ground as with herbaceous types. It is excellent for sagebrush-steppe or Intermountain West gardens mimicking its native scabland habitat.

planting.note: Direct-sow in fall with cold stratification into well-drained decomposed granite or gravelly loam; give afternoon shade in hot lowland gardens.

directions: A compact high-elevation Sierra Nevada and Cascade native with blue flowers, this species is a documented host plant for roughly ten native lepidoptera species. It is best suited to higher-elevation or cooler-summer gardens replicating its native 4,900-to-9,800-foot range; in hot lowland gardens give it afternoon shade. Combine with other subalpine natives rather than lowland xeriscape companions that want more heat.

planting.note: Direct-sow in fall with 4-8 weeks cold stratification into lean, rocky, fast-draining soil matching sagebrush shrubland or woodland-edge conditions.

directions: Showy large blue-violet flowers with contrasting violet nectar guides decorate this tidy plant, native to rocky Wyoming and Montana sagebrush and woodland edges, well suited to high-plains xeriscape. Give it the same lean, rocky, fast-draining soil it uses in sagebrush shrublands and juniper or Douglas-fir woodland edges — rich garden loam shortens its life substantially. It blooms over an unusually long window from May through August when not stressed by excess water.

planting.note: Direct-sow in spring, or root cuttings, into average garden soil in full sun to light shade; tolerates occasional summer irrigation better than most native penstemons.

directions: Described as more garden-tolerant than most native penstemons, this species forms a tidy bluish-green mound with vivid blue tubular flowers, making it a good container and border candidate for Northern California and Oregon gardens. Unlike many high-alpine penstemons, it tolerates occasional summer irrigation and average garden soil, making it a good gateway native penstemon for gardeners new to the genus. It is deer resistant and attracts bees and hummingbirds, and works well in mixed borders, not just scree or rock gardens.

planting.note: Direct-sow in fall with cold stratification into lean, well-drained soil matching sagebrush-steppe conditions; shear lightly after bloom to keep the tuft tidy.

directions: Distinctive narrow, needle-like, larch-like foliage forms a grassy tuft quite unlike typical broadleaf penstemons, with cream, pink, or purple flowers attracting hummingbirds. Its fine, conifer-like foliage makes it a valuable textural foil next to broadleaf penstemons and succulents in a rock garden. Native to the northern Rockies, it wants the same lean, well-drained soil as its sagebrush-steppe companions.

planting.note: Sow about 2 months before last frost with very light seed cover into lean, gravelly or rocky soil; clay soil is reliably fatal to this species over winter.

directions: A Colorado Front Range foothills staple, this species forms a neat evergreen cushion topped with blue, lavender-throated flower spikes in May and is one of the easiest native penstemons to start from seed. Site at the very front of a border or in a rock garden, since its diminutive cushion habit is easily lost behind taller plants. Lean, gravelly or rocky soil is essential; clay soil reliably kills this species over winter.

planting.note: Divide clumps in spring, or stratify seed 3 months at 40F, into a sharply drained site; winter wet is more damaging than cold.

directions: A branched, semi-evergreen shrubby penstemon from the western interior with blue, pink, or white flower variation and good coastal tolerance, this species offers four-season structure most herbaceous penstemons lack. It dislikes winter wet more than cold, so a sharply drained site is more important than extra winter protection. Good as a cutting-garden or border plant, not just a rock-garden specimen.
